title: To your past self
hookLine: write to the you who suffered most

lines: SEVEN SHIPS ON A STRANGE BEACH.
A SENTENCE AIMED AT THE FUTURE.
cards: Seven battered ships have been dragged up on a beach nobody recognizes. Men soaked and shaking, the rest of the fleet scattered by the storm. This is the opening of Virgil's Aeneid, the Roman epic.
The hero, Aeneas, has to say something to his men. He has no good news. He doesn't know where they are or whether the others are alive.
So he says something strange: a sentence aimed at a future none of them can see yet.

teach.h: PERHAPS ONE DAY IT WILL HELP TO REMEMBER.
teach.b: First, the line. In Latin, forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit. Put plainly: perhaps one day it will help to remember even this.
Not that it's fine. Not that it happened for a reason. Only that someday, looking back, remembering this hour may bring something like gladness.
The man who survives it will see it differently than the man inside it. Second, what Aeneas hides. Virgil adds a detail right after the speech.

teach.h: HOPE ON HIS FACE, GRIEF IN HIS HEART.
teach.b: Aeneas wears hope on his face, and presses his grief down deep in his heart. He is sick at heart with huge cares of his own. The future self he points to is also the self he needs.
Third, turn it around. Aeneas spoke from inside the storm toward a future he couldn't see.

teach.h: NOW YOU STAND ON THE FAR SIDE.
teach.b: Today, you may be the one standing on the far side, looking back. Somewhere behind you is the version of you who had the hardest time: a year, a night, a hospital corridor, a move, a loss.
That person couldn't know that you would be sitting here, on day seven hundred fifty-five of a practice, breathing. You can know it. Fourth, what to write.
Not advice; that person has heard enough advice, and a couple of weeks ago this path put presence before solutions. Not a lecture about what they should have done.
Something closer to Aeneas: company, and a report from the future. Three lines is enough. Some people find words like: I see you.
It was as hard as it felt.

how: Some people write letters to their younger selves in journals, in therapy, or on anniversaries of a hard time, offering the company they didn't have then rather than advice.

o: the Roman poet who wrote the epic of the storm
Virgil's hero, who said one day it may help to remember
the Greek hero who sailed home from Troy for ten years

games.q: what's inside Aeneas's beach — tap the pairs.
p: the Roman poet of the Aeneid
the hero who speaks to his men
grief pressed down in his heart

s: Aeneas tells his men the storm happened for a reason
he says only that perhaps one day it will help to remember even this.
Virgil says Aeneas hides his own grief while he speaks
hope on his face, grief pressed deep in his heart.
a letter to your past self should explain what they did wrong
today's letter is company and a report from the future, not a lecture.

games.q: you're Aeneas. your men are soaked and shaking on a strange beach, the rest of the fleet scattered. you have no good news. what do you say?
o: tell them the truth: we're finished.
perhaps one day it will help to remember even this.
games.why: he speaks to a future they can't see yet, while hiding his own grief: hope on his face, grief in his heart.

practice: Let the you who suffered most come to mind, just how old they were and where, without reliving it; just see them from here.
Then write three lines to them, starting with their name or with dear me: what you see in them, something true about now, and, if it fits, you made it here.
When you're done, put the pen down and sit with them for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: Aeneas, Virgil's hero on a strange beach, telling his men that one day it may help to remember even this. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: you made it here. The far side of a storm can speak back to the one inside it. That's day seven hundred fifty-five.
